text:
Elliot (solutions): Heads-up, ACME POC: logs are landing in Splunk but traces aren't joining up. We have request_id present but no trace_id/traceparent in indexed events. Anyone seen this flow before?
Tanya (account): Customer escalating a SOC check — they want a quick root cause and mitigation.
Rob (infra): Typical culprits: header stripped at ingress, a sidecar normalization, or the forwarder losing events during HEC rate spikes. What headers are you sending?
Elliot (solutions): We send both `traceparent` and `x-redwood-trace`. ALB shows them, but Splunk events don't. I grabbed an ALB sample: `traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`
Rob (infra): Ok check 3 places in order: 1) ingress (nginx/envoy) access_log, 2) app sidecar (TLS terminator) behavior, 3) forwarder parsing. If header gone at nginx, it's upstream. If present in nginx but missing in forwarder, it's likely transform.
Elliot (solutions): Ran `grep` on nginx access.log — header absent there. ALB log has header. So something between ALB and nginx is rewriting. Customer uses an AWS NLB -> WAF -> nginx chain. WAF can drop non-standard headers.
Tanya (account): They can't change WAF rules immediately. Is there a POC-safe workaround we can propose so they can keep correlation for dashboards?
Rob (infra): Two non-invasive options while they fix WAF rules: A) Use an allowed header name (e.g., `x-request-id`) that WAF passes through and map it to trace in the forwarder; B) synthesize a trace id in the forwarder from the existing request_id. Option A is better if they want a real propagated id. Example: client sets `x-request-id: r-12345` and we map it to `trace_id` in the forwarder pipeline.
Elliot (solutions): Do you have an example forwarder remap for Vector or Fluentd? I can give that to their SRE.
Rob (infra): Sure, Vector remap example (pseudo):

    transforms.rx_map.type = "remap"
    transforms.rx_map.source = '''
      .trace_id = if exists(.headers["x-redwood-trace"]) { .headers["x-redwood-trace"] } else if exists(.headers["x-request-id"]) { .headers["x-request-id"] } else { null }
    '''

And a fallback synthesizer:

    transforms.synth.type = "lua"
    transforms.synth.script = '''
      function process(event)
        if not event.trace_id and event.request_id then
          event.trace_id = event.request_id
        end
        return event
      end
    '''

This keeps correlation for dashboards while WAF is updated.
Tanya (account): ACME is worried about accuracy vs compliance. Will synthesizing IDs create compliance issues?
Rob (infra): No, synthesized ids are derived from existing request_ids already in logs. Our redaction rules still run. We can produce a config snapshot proving REDWOOD_REDACT_FIELDS was set during the POC.
Elliot (solutions): We also saw bursts of 429s reported by the forwarder around the same time traces were missing. Could dropped events explain partial traces?
Rob (infra): Absolutely. If child span events are dropped, you'll have orphaned root logs. The forwarder logs show `HTTP 429` to the customer's HEC endpoint between 23:05-23:40. We should either buffer/retry or request a temporary HEC throttle increase. Suggested envs for the forwarder: `FORWARDER_BUFFER_SIZE=150MB` and `FORWARDER_MAX_RETRIES=6`.
Tanya (account): Does buffering add cost or risk? Customer asked if enabling retries could duplicate events and mess up billing.
Rob (infra): Retries can create duplicates if the HEC endpoint is not idempotent. Splunk HEC is usually idempotent for JSON events if you use a dedupe key, but many customers accept small duplication during POC. We can enable de-duplication on ingest or set the forwarder to use a dedupe hash. For POC short-term, duplications are typically acceptable.
Elliot (solutions): Can we add a quick smoke test so SREs can validate header propagation and HEC health?
Rob (infra): Yes. Two commands for SRE: 

  1) header echo: `curl -H "x-redwood-trace: poc-xyz-001" -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" https://api.redwood.example.com/v1/debug/header-echo` -> response must include x-redwood-trace.
  2) Splunk search: `index=acme trace_id="poc-xyz-001" | head 20` (should return within 60s).

Also add an ingest alert: `forwarder_429_rate > 5/min for 5m -> page infra`.
Tanya (account): ACME has a change window at 21:00 PST tonight to touch WAF rules. If they can't get it, they'll accept the forwarder remap. Is that acceptable?
Rob (infra): Yes. I'll draft a short playbook for them to follow and a sample Vector remap file. I'll also attach the redaction snapshot and note on synthetic trace limitations for SOC: synthesised ids link logs but won't reconstruct parent/span trees.
logbot: alert: forwarder.acme.hec 429 spike detected 2026-03-20T23:08Z -> 35m (avg 9/min)
Elliot (solutions): Great. Can you commit the playbook and the sample remap and I'll paste into the deal ticket?
deploy-bot: release/poc-acme-playbook v2026-03-22.1 rolled to dedicated/us-west-2 at 2026-03-22T03:00:00Z
Rob (infra): Playbook posted to the ticket: steps -> validate header at ALB, validate nginx access_log, apply Vector remap or synth transform, increase forwarder buffer/retries or request HEC bump, run smoke tests, and close.
Tanya (account): I'll send the SOC language: "By default traces do not contain PII; redaction was enabled during the POC; header-based correlation is preserved unless an intermediary rewrites headers; we provided a playbook and remedial transforms so correlation can be recovered for the POC."
Elliot (solutions): Closing loop — customer agreed to either WAF change tonight or remap tomorrow morning. Will reopen if any other failures show up. Thanks all.
